recommendations.improvement_summary_text: 50 mm internal or external wall insulation
recommendations.improvement_descr_text: Solid wall insulation involves adding a layer of insulation to either the inside or the outside surface of the external walls, which reduces heat loss and lowers fuel bills. As it is more expensive than cavity wall insulation it is only recommended for walls without a cavity, or where for technical reasons a cavity cannot be filled. Internal insulation, known as dry-lining, is where a layer of insulation is fixed to the inside surface of external walls; this type of insulation is best applied when rooms require redecorating and can be installed by a competent DIY enthusiast. External solid wall insulation is the application of an insulant and a weather-protective finish to the outside of the wall. This may improve the look of the home, particularly where existing brickwork or rendering is poor, and will provide long-lasting weather protection. Further information can be obtained from the National Insulation Association (www.nationalinsulationassociation.org.uk).

recommendations.improvement_summary_text: Replace single glazed windows with low-E double glazed windows
recommendations.improvement_descr_text: Double glazing is the term given to a system where two panes of glass are made up into a sealed unit. Replacing existing single-glazed windows with double-glazed windows will improve comfort in the home by reducing draughts and cold spots near windows. Double-glazed windows may also reduce noise, improve security and combat problems with condensation.

Insulation of a floor will significantly reduce heat loss; this will improve levels of comfort, reduce energy use and lower fuel bills. Suspended floors can often be insulated from below. . Further information about floor insulation is available from many sources including www.energysavingtrust.org.uk/northernireland/Insulation/Floor-insulation.

A solar PV system is one which converts light directly into electricity via panels placed on the roof with no waste and no emissions. This electricity is used throughout the home in the same way as the electricity purchased from an energy supplier. The British Photovoltaic Association has up-to-date information on local installers who are qualified electricians. It is best to obtain advice from a qualified electrician. Ask the electrician to explain the options.

Fitting draught proofing, strips of insulation around windows and doors, will improve the comfort in the home. A contractor can be employed but draught proofing can be installed by a competent DIY enthusiast.

surveyTasks.method: Photograph front, side, valves and model label. Measure dimensions, panel/convector or column count and pipe outside diameter. Record obstructions and homeowner constraints.

surveyTasks.title: Find all remaining emitters
surveyTasks.why: The four photo observations are an incomplete inventory.
surveyTasks.method: Walk every room, including halls, bathrooms and lower ground; link each emitter or confirmed absence to a stable room ID.

surveyTasks.title: Locate meter, consumer unit and supply route
surveyTasks.why: Meter position alone does not establish a suitable electrical connection.
surveyTasks.method: Qualified electrical assessment: locate meter, service and consumer unit; record supply capacity, earthing, spare ways and a feasible protected cable route.

fields.label: Electrical assessor findings and remaining checks

surveyTasks.title: Locate existing hot-water equipment and cylinder options
surveyTasks.why: Cylinder volume, access, support and recovery requirements depend on the house and household.
surveyTasks.method: Identify existing system, available cupboard dimensions, delivery route, structural support, drainage and connections; ask about hot-water use.

fields.label: Occupancy and hot-water use; evidence source

surveyTasks.title: Measure outdoor siting options
surveyTasks.why: Usable ground, sound, airflow, servicing, drains and routing constrain location.
surveyTasks.method: Compare rear courtyard options with homeowners; measure available envelope and routes, drainage, neighbour receptors and obstacles. Check selected manufacturer and current applicable siting requirements.

fields.label: Clearances, noise, drainage, access and checks still required

surveyTasks.title: Trace hydraulic and electrical routes
surveyTasks.why: Straight-line distances miss walls, level changes, access and hydraulic resistance.
surveyTasks.method: Record separate route segments from outdoor unit to hydraulic/cylinder connections, heating circuit, consumer unit and condensate discharge. Mark length, vertical rise, diameter, fittings, penetrations and access.

fields.label: Endpoint IDs and measured route segments

surveyTasks.title: Record homeowner choices and constraints
surveyTasks.why: Layout and equipment changes need explicit household choices.
surveyTasks.method: Discuss comfort, rooms used, hot-water habits, refurbishment plans, outdoor space, cylinder storage trade-offs, radiator appearance and disruption. Record preferred alternatives separately from technical approval.

fields.label: Named option IDs, preferences and unresolved choices

options.title: Outdoor unit near rear courtyard
options.tradeoff: Potentially short route to rear kitchen; compare noise, airflow, garden use and service access.

options.title: Cylinder in lower-ground utility area
options.tradeoff: May preserve upstairs storage; access, headroom, support, drainage and route remain unknown.

options.title: Alternative internal cylinder space
options.tradeoff: Survey other cupboards; compare delivery access, storage loss and connection distances.

limits: Sensitivity scenarios, not confidence intervals or equipment selections.
Room areas include wall/void uncertainty; upper rear room ceiling heights are especially uncertain.
Main side runs assumed party at 18°C; rear wings assumed exposed.
Basement exposed walls assumed 30% air / 70% ground at 10°C; openings outside.
Cool basement is an imposed 11°C boundary hypothesis, not an equilibrium calculation.
All emitters remain unmeasured until output evidence is supplied.
Thermal bridges use an explicit 0.05–0.15 W/m²K envelope allowance.
Heat pump performance, annual energy, grants and regulatory approval are not calculated.
